title: Conflict Management
sequence: Throughout the project, most visibly in Executing. Ground rules are set early (team charter); conflict is addressed as soon as it appears.

header.html: People domain (33%) · Task 2 Manage conflicts — identify conflict sources · analyze the context for the conflict · implement an agreed-on resolution strategy · communicate conflict management principles with the team and external stakeholders · establish an environment that fosters adherence to common ground rules · manage and rectify ground rule violations

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Conflict Inevitable in a project environment. Sources include scarce resources, scheduling priorities and personal work styles
Conflict management Anticipating, addressing and resolving conflict so it leads to greater productivity and positive working relationships; managed well, differences of opinion can increase creativity and better decision-making
Ground rules Expectations about acceptable behavior by team members (and other stakeholders regarding engagement), defined in the team charter
Group norms Shared unwritten or written behaviors the team follows; with ground rules, role definition and communication planning they reduce conflict
Resolution technique Withdraw/avoid, smooth/accommodate, compromise/reconcile, force/direct, collaborate/problem-solve
Facilitation Guiding a group event to a successful decision, solution or conclusion, with full participation and buy-in
Negotiation A discussion aimed at reaching agreement, to gain support or resolve conflicts within the team or with stakeholders
Escalation Moving an unresolved matter to someone with more authority (the PM, management, formal procedures)

2Manage Conflicts: the Process

Core rules (PMBOK 8):

  • Address conflict early, usually in private, using a direct, collaborative approach.
  • Team members are initially responsible for resolving a conflict that becomes a negative factor. If it escalates, the project manager helps facilitate a satisfactory resolution.
  • If disruptive conflict continues, formal procedures may be used, including disciplinary actions.
  • A project manager's success often depends on the ability to resolve conflicts.

3Identify Conflict Sources (ECO)

Source Examples
Scarce resources Two projects or teams competing for the same specialist, equipment or budget
Scheduling priorities Different views on what comes first; conflicting due dates
Personal work styles Preferences for planning, communication, pace, detail
Administrative procedures and policies Beyond PMBOK 8 Conflicting approval routes, document standards or reporting rules
Personality clashes Beyond PMBOK 8 Friction between individuals unrelated to the task; address behavior and the work, not the person
Roles and accountability Beyond PMBOK 8 Two parties believe they own the same work, or nobody does (a RACI with no single accountable owner)
Requirements and expectations Hidden or contradictory expectations, even from the same signed document
Technical or approach differences Different views on solution, tools or methods
Incentives and objectives Bonuses or goals that reward opposing behaviors (speed vs thoroughness)
Communication and culture Misreadings, language, culture, remote working
Change Reorganization, new members, scope or process change, an undocumented informal change

Find the real source before acting. A symptom (an argument) often hides a cause (an undefined handoff, an informal change nobody recorded, a gap in accountability). Trace the dispute back to its origin, then fix the cause rather than only negotiating the symptom.

4Analyze the Context (ECO)

PMBOK 8 lists the factors that influence the choice of method:

  1. Importance and intensity of the conflict.
  2. Time pressure for resolving it.
  3. Relative power of the people involved.
  4. Importance of maintaining a good relationship.
  5. Motivation to resolve it in the long or short term.

Also consider [Beyond PMBOK 8]: who is involved (team, stakeholders, vendors); whether the positions are both sound; whether there is a safety, compliance or ethics element; whether the cause is structural (roles, incentives, processes) or personal; and what has already been tried.

5Implement an Agreed Resolution Strategy (ECO)

Technique What it is Outcome Typical use
Collaborate / problem-solve Incorporate multiple viewpoints and insights; cooperative attitude and open dialogue Consensus and commitment; win-win Important issue, time available, relationships matter; preferred when feasible
Compromise / reconcile Search for solutions that bring some satisfaction to all parties, temporarily or partially Occasionally lose-lose Time pressure, equal power, both positions sound
Force / direct Push your viewpoint at others' expense, often using a power position Win-lose Emergencies; safety and compliance; a necessary decision
Smooth / accommodate Emphasize agreement; concede to maintain harmony and relationships Preserves relationship The issue matters little to you, or the relationship matters more
Withdraw / avoid Retreat from or postpone the conflict Delays resolution Trivial issues, high emotion (cool down first), need for preparation, or someone else is better placed to resolve it

Source note: PMBOK 8 defines the five techniques and the outcomes shown (win-win, win-lose, occasionally lose-lose) and says each "has its place and use". The Typical use column is exam-practice guidance Beyond PMBOK 8.

How to run the resolution:

  1. Create a safe space and keep communication open and respectful (words, tone and body language).
  2. Focus on the issues, not the people; conflict arises because people perceive situations differently, so do not assign blame.
  3. Focus on the present and future, not the past; reviving old events can intensify the conflict.
  4. Search for alternatives together, moving the conflict into a problem-solving space.
  5. Facilitate an agreement, document who will do what, and follow up.
  6. Escalate in steps: the parties involved, the PM facilitating, management or the sponsor (for objectives and incentives beyond your authority), formal procedures.

Examples of matching technique to situation:

  • Two sound positions and a window that closes in two days → compromise (collaboration needs time the window does not allow).
  • Two defensible dates expected by two directors → facilitate a joint session to agree one date, rather than more analysis.
  • Opposing incentives drive repeated clashes → work with the functional managers to align objectives; mediation alone treats the symptom.
  • An emergency or safety call → direct decision by the authorized person.
  • A conflict between stakeholders who each assume the project is mainly for them → a facilitated workshop to agree priorities.
  • Signed requirements read differently → facilitate a discussion; the text cannot settle it.

6Communicate Conflict Management Principles (ECO)

  • Tell people the rules of the game early: how disagreements will be raised and resolved, who facilitates, when and how matters escalate. Put them in the team charter (conflict resolution process), the communications plan and, for vendors and partners, the agreements (including dispute resolution clauses; Topic 22).
  • State the four principles: open and respectful communication; issues not people; present and future; alternatives together.
  • Include external stakeholders: share the escalation path and expectations at kickoff and when new parties join; hold them to agreements through their management.
  • Model the behavior: transparency, integrity, respect, positive discourse (dialogue, not debate), support and courage (Topic 25).
  • Preventive practices that reduce conflict: ground rules and norms, communication planning, role definition, clear priorities, visible decisions and shared objectives.

7Establish an Environment That Fosters Adherence to Ground Rules (ECO)

  • Co-create them (the team charter works best when the team develops it), covering values, communication, decision-making, conflict resolution, meeting guidelines and agreements.
  • Everyone shares responsibility for following them; leaders follow them first.
  • Reinforce them consistently: recognize adherence, apply them to everyone, remind people when drifting.
  • Revisit them when new members join (they should help shape the rules rather than be handed them privately) and when the context changes (for example virtual working, new vendor).
  • Safe environment: people speak up when they will not be punished for candor.
  • Apply them to external parties through briefings and agreements.

8Manage and Rectify Ground Rule Violations (ECO)

Step What to do
1. Notice early Watch behavior, retrospectives and feedback for drift; address small breaches before they grow
2. Talk privately Describe what you saw factually; listen to the person's reason; do not assume motives
3. Refer to the agreement Remind the person of the rule the team created; agree what will change
4. Involve the team when the rule is theirs A team-made charter is best addressed by the team, with the PM facilitating (a team discussion on honoring the agreement), rather than by individual enforcement or a new imposed process
5. Coach and follow up Support the person, check progress, recognize improvement
6. Fix the system If the rule is unclear, missing or unworkable, update the charter with the team
7. Use the formal route when needed Repeated or serious breaches go through management or HR procedures; ethics or compliance violations follow organizational policy and the PMI Code (Topic 06)
8. External parties Raise breaches with their management and refer to the agreement and escalation path

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Ground rules Team charter and organizational policy; PM enforces within authority Working agreements owned by the team; revisited in retrospectives Charter for the whole; working agreements inside teams
First responders Parties, then the PM and functional managers The team first; servant leader facilitates; product owner for priority conflicts Both
Priority conflicts Change control and sponsor or governance decisions Product owner orders the backlog by value, with visibility to all Both
Escalation Defined chain: PM, sponsor, steering committee, formal procedures Team, then facilitator or PM, then management for impediments beyond the team Mix
Forum for issues Status and issue meetings Daily coordination, retrospectives Both

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor to team maturity (storming is normal), culture (directness varies), authority structure (weak matrix: align functional managers), virtual working, criticality and the number of parties.
  • Interactions: conflict links to stakeholder engagement (expectations), resources (scarcity, roles), communication (misunderstanding), procurement (claims and disputes), quality (disagreements about standards) and governance (escalation thresholds).
  • Signs of effective conflict management: conflicts are raised early and openly; resolutions are agreed and hold; relationships and productivity are maintained; ground rules are followed; ideas from disagreement improve decisions.

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Find the source first. The visible argument is rarely the cause; trace it (an undocumented change, an unclear handoff, a missing accountable owner).
  2. Collaborate when time and importance allow; compromise when time is short and both positions are sound; force only for emergencies or safety; avoid or smooth only for minor issues or cooling off.
  3. Address conflict early, privately and directly, not in front of the team and not after it explodes.
  4. Team members try first; the PM facilitates if it escalates; formal procedures if it stays disruptive.
  5. Focus on issues, not people, and on the present and future, not the past.
  6. Alignment of objectives beats mediation when incentives conflict: involve the managers who set them.
  7. A team-made charter is enforced by the team, with the PM facilitating; do not issue a new rule or lecture privately.
  8. New members help shape ground rules; revisit the agreement with the whole team.
  9. Both parties signed the same document and still disagree? Facilitate a discussion; re-reading the text will not settle it.
  10. Hidden expectations: surface and align them before baselining or committing.
  11. Fix the role gap: if two parties are "responsible" and nobody is accountable, update the RAM.
  12. Ground rules also apply to vendors and partners: put them in agreements; escalate through their management.
  13. Do not ignore, hide or punish: silence and public blame make conflict worse.
  14. Ethics or legal violations are not "conflicts to compromise"; follow policy and the Code.
  15. Document agreements and follow up; check that the resolution holds.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Two technical leads from different scrum teams disagree about a data-migration strategy. Both positions have merit, there are two weeks before the decision is needed, and the leads must work together for a year. What should the project manager do?

  • APostpone the decision and let the leads settle it informally over time
  • BSplit the difference at once by combining half of each proposal
  • CChoose the strategy that the more senior lead proposed and inform both leads
  • DFacilitate collaborative problem-solving that addresses both leads' concerns
Show the answer

Answer: D. The issue is important, time is available and the relationship matters, which favors collaboration and a win-win solution. Deciding for them, splitting the difference immediately or leaving it informal gives up the chance for real commitment.

S2Two reviewers want different color schemes for a customer banner. Both are acceptable, they have equal standing, and the print file is due in two hours. What is the best approach?

  • AImpose the project manager's own preference without any discussion
  • BStart a multi-day design workshop to build consensus on the color scheme
  • CAgree a scheme that partly satisfies both reviewers right now, which is a compromise
  • DLet the printer pick a scheme, withdrawing from the disagreement
Show the answer

Answer: C. With equal power, two acceptable options and a short deadline, compromise resolves the matter in time, whereas collaboration needs time the deadline does not allow. Imposing a choice or withdrawing gives up the relationship or the control.

S3A sales director and the quality lead disagree: sales wants to ship units that failed a mandatory safety test to meet an order date, and suggests shipping only half as a compromise. What should the project manager do?

  • ASmooth the disagreement by agreeing to review the test results after shipment
  • BCollaborate on a shipping plan that satisfies the order date and the quality lead
  • CAccept the compromise of half the units, which both parties can live with
  • DRefuse to ship the failed units and escalate under policy
Show the answer

Answer: D. A mandatory safety requirement is not a conflict to compromise: the project manager follows the policy, protects people and escalates through governance. Shipping some failed units, designing a plan around them or deferring review all accept noncompliance.

S4A valued stakeholder insists on a specific font for internal slides. The project manager does not care about the font but values the relationship. Which technique fits?

  • ASmooth or accommodate, conceding the minor point to maintain the relationship
  • BForce, by telling the stakeholder that the project's template must be used
  • CCollaborate, by running a workshop to find the ideal font for the slides
  • DWithdraw, by postponing the slide discussion until the stakeholder gives in
Show the answer

Answer: A. When the issue matters little and the relationship matters more, smoothing or accommodating is appropriate. Forcing, collaborating at length or withdrawing spends effort or goodwill on a minor point.

S5In a facilitated session between two leads, one keeps recalling an error the other made last year. What should the project manager do?

  • ALet the lead finish, since the history explains the conflict between them
  • BRedirect the talk to the present issue and future alternatives
  • CAsk the other lead to apologize for the old error in front of the group
  • DEnd the session and decide the issue without either lead's input
Show the answer

Answer: B. Conflict is handled by focusing on issues rather than people and on the present and future rather than the past, since reviving old events intensifies it. Letting the history run, demanding an apology or ending the session leaves the real issue unresolved.

S6Two team members' hostility continues despite facilitated sessions and several retrospectives, and it is now hurting the team's output. What is the next step?

  • AIgnore the hostility and focus on the output of the remaining members
  • BMove one of the two members to another team without informing management
  • CInvolve management and use formal procedures, which may include disciplinary action
  • DKeep facilitating the same kind of session weekly until the hostility stops
Show the answer

Answer: C. If disruptive conflict continues after team members and the project manager have tried to resolve it, formal procedures, including disciplinary actions through management, may be used. Repeating the same approach, ignoring it or moving someone unilaterally does not follow the escalation path.

S7A subcontractor's crew keeps bypassing the agreed escalation path and calls the sponsor directly with complaints. What should the project manager do?

  • AAccept the direct calls, since the sponsor is the most senior contact
  • BRaise it with the subcontractor's management under the agreed path
  • CTell the sponsor to refuse the calls and refer the crew to the project manager
  • DRemove the crew from the site until the subcontractor changes its behavior
Show the answer

Answer: B. Ground rules apply to vendors through the agreement, so breaches are raised with the vendor's management and the escalation path is reinforced. Having the sponsor refuse calls, accepting the bypass or removing the crew skips the agreed route.

S8A member routinely joins the daily coordination meeting ten minutes late, contrary to the working agreement, and the others are irritated. What should the project manager do first?

  • AChange the meeting time to suit the member without consulting the team
  • BAsk the team to vote on a penalty for anyone who arrives late
  • CTalk with the member privately, learn the reason and refer to the agreement
  • DAnnounce at the next meeting that latecomers will be recorded in the minutes
Show the answer

Answer: C. Rule violations are addressed early, privately and factually: understand the reason, refer to the agreement, agree steps and, if the rule proves unworkable, update it with the team. Public warnings, penalties or unilateral changes skip the conversation.

S9During a retrospective, two team members begin shouting at each other. What should the project manager do?

  • AReprimand both members in front of the team to restore order
  • BContinue the retrospective and address the matter at the end of the session
  • CMake them settle it in front of the team immediately to clear the air
  • DPause the session to let emotions cool, then speak with each privately
Show the answer

Answer: D. Withdrawing temporarily lets emotions settle, and the conflict is then addressed early, privately and collaboratively. Forcing a public resolution, carrying on or a public reprimand escalates the situation.

S10After a negotiation over sprint priorities, both departments gave up part of what they wanted and neither is satisfied. Which technique and outcome does this describe?

  • ACompromise, which can occasionally leave both sides losing
  • BSmoothing, which preserves the relationship at no cost to either side
  • CForce, which produces a win-lose result in favor of one side only
  • DCollaboration, which always produces a win-win result for both sides
Show the answer

Answer: A. Compromise brings some satisfaction to all parties but can occasionally be lose-lose, as here. Collaboration aims at win-win, force is win-lose and smoothing concedes to maintain harmony.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1What are the five conflict resolution techniques?

Show the answer

Withdraw/avoid, smooth/accommodate, compromise/reconcile, force/direct, collaborate/problem-solve.

R2Which technique is likely to produce win-win, win-lose and lose-lose?

Show the answer

Collaborate: win-win. Force: win-lose. Compromise: occasionally lose-lose.

R3What are the typical sources of conflict according to PMBOK 8?

Show the answer

Scarce resources, scheduling priorities and personal work styles.

R4What factors influence the choice of resolution method?

Show the answer

Importance and intensity, time pressure, relative power, importance of the relationship, and motivation to resolve it in the long or short term.

R5How should conflict be addressed, and who is first responsible?

Show the answer

Early, usually in private, with a direct, collaborative approach. Team members are initially responsible; the PM facilitates if it escalates.

R6What if disruptive conflict continues?

Show the answer

Formal procedures may be used, including disciplinary actions.

R7What are the four principles for handling conflict?

Show the answer

Keep communication open and respectful; focus on the issues, not the people; focus on the present and future, not the past; search for alternatives together.

R8What are ground rules and where are they defined?

Show the answer

Expectations of acceptable behavior by team members and stakeholders, defined in the team charter.

R9How can conflict be reduced proactively?

Show the answer

Ground rules, group norms, communication planning and role definition.

R10What are the positive effects of well-managed conflict?

Show the answer

Greater productivity and positive relationships, increased creativity and better decision-making.

R11When is withdrawing appropriate?

Show the answer

For trivial issues, to let emotions cool, or when more preparation is needed; the issue should be revisited.

R12How do you handle a violation of a team-made charter?

Show the answer

Address it promptly and privately, refer to the agreement, involve the team in honoring it, coach and follow up, and use formal channels for repeated or serious breaches.

R13Who should lead resolution when positions are both sound but a deadline is near?

Show the answer

The project manager, using compromise to resolve it in time.

R14What should be done before choosing a resolution strategy?

Show the answer

Identify the source of the conflict and analyze its context.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Sources Scarce resources, scheduling priorities, work styles; also roles, incentives, requirements, change
Context factors Importance and intensity, time pressure, relative power, relationship, long or short term
Techniques Collaborate (win-win), compromise, force/direct (win-lose), smooth/accommodate, withdraw/avoid
Default Address early, usually private, direct and collaborative
Who Parties first; PM facilitates if escalated; formal procedures if disruptive
Principles Open and respectful; issues not people; present and future; alternatives together
Ground rules Expected behavior in the team charter; co-created; revisited with new members
Violation Private, factual, refer to the agreement, team involvement, coach, formal route if repeated
External parties Rules in agreements and kickoff; escalate through their management
Root cause first Trace undocumented changes, unclear handoffs and accountability gaps
Incentive conflicts Align objectives with functional managers
Emergency or safety Force/direct by the authorized person
Time pressure with sound positions Compromise
First-action pattern Find the source, analyze the context, pick the technique, facilitate an agreement, document and follow up, fix the system
